episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Thursday, March 19, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education.
-
Today, universities launch A.I. initiatives from coast to coast, while faculty survey data reveals deep concerns about student critical thinking.
-
In Insights and Trends today, Lawyers Hub has launched the Africa A.I. Policy Fellowship, a three-month program designed to develop emerging and mid-career professionals in artificial intelligence governance.

According to Global South Opportunities, the fellowship combines academic training, mentorship, and hands-on policy engagement. It targets policy analysts, legal professionals, researchers, academics, and technology specialists. The program explicitly focuses on developing policy recommendations tailored to African contexts, recognizing that A.I. governance frameworks developed in other regions may not directly translate. The three-month intensive format targets working professionals who need focused, practical training rather than comprehensive degree programs.
-
Also in Insights and Trends, an NPR report finds college faculty and students are creating divergent A.I. policies in their classrooms.

According to NPR, Professor Dan Cryer at Johnson County Community College opposes A.I. in writing, comparing it to, quote, bringing a forklift to the gym, end quote. In contrast, Professor Leslie Clement at Johnson C. Smith University embraces A.I. as a, quote, powerful collaborator, end quote, and co-created a course on African Diaspora and A.I. The contrast illustrates how individual instructors are navigating A.I. integration with vastly different philosophies.
-
In another Insights and Trends story, College Board research surveying more than 3,000 faculty finds 74 percent report students using A.I. to write essays.

According to the College Board, 84 percent of faculty agree A.I. reduces critical thinking and originality among students. Faculty at selective institutions and writing-intensive disciplines express significantly greater concerns than STEM and business faculty. The data suggests a disciplinary divide in how faculty perceive A.I.'s impact on student learning.
-
Turning to Case Studies, Washington University is launching +AI, a universitywide initiative led by Provost Mark D. West to balance A.I.'s potential with the university's commitment to student formation.

According to The Source, the initiative includes an A.I. Literacy Module for undergraduates, new generative A.I. tools including Gemini for Education and NotebookLM, and an AI Curriculum Corps for faculty. +AI Perspectives Week on March 23 will feature Nicholas Thompson, CEO of The Atlantic, discussing A.I.'s impact on graduates and employment. Provost West stated the university will ask hard questions and put human judgment at the center.
-
In another Case Study, Cornell has appointed Professor Thorsten Joachims as Vice Provost for Artificial Intelligence Strategy, signaling institutional commitment to A.I. integration.

According to The Cornell Daily Sun, the HiTA platform is deployed in language and computer science courses, providing hints rather than direct answers to encourage deeper learning. Spanish courses use Chitter Chatter as an A.I. conversation partner. Professor Kizilcec noted that unlike consumer A.I. designed to give fast answers, educational A.I. should encourage deeper learning.
-
In Practical Tips, the UCI Digital Learning Lab and School of Education will launch an Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education course for instructors starting summer 2026.

According to New University, the online course will be delivered synchronously over Zoom. It is tailored for faculty, lecturers, and supporting staff seeking to integrate A.I. into their teaching.
-
Also in Practical Tips, UNC's College of Arts and Sciences has launched an initiative to enhance A.I. literacy among students through collaboration between University Libraries and the Department of English.

According to UNC College of Arts and Sciences, the Carolina AI Literacy Initiative offers videos and modules guiding users through A.I. basics, composing effective prompts, recognizing bias, fact-checking output, and avoiding plagiarism.
-
That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

topStory.headline: Lawyers Hub Launches Africa A.I. Policy Fellowship for Governance Professionals
topStory.summary:
Lawyers Hub has launched the Africa A.I. Policy Fellowship, a three-month program designed to develop emerging and mid-career professionals in artificial intelligence governance and regulatory frameworks, according to Global South Opportunities. The fellowship combines academic training, mentorship, and hands-on policy engagement, targeting policy analysts, legal professionals, researchers, academics, technology specialists, and development practitioners.

The program explicitly focuses on developing policy recommendations tailored to African contexts, recognizing that A.I. governance frameworks developed in other regions may not directly translate. The fellowship emphasizes bridging the gap between academic learning and real-world policy engagement.

The application process is designed to be accessible at seven minutes, and the three-month intensive format targets working professionals who need focused, practical training rather than comprehensive degree programs. The fellowship emphasizes building networks of professionals capable of influencing national and regional policy discussions.
